Windisch,’ on the other hand, attempted to prove a close
similarity between the plot of the political side of the play and

attaining the throne, the jealousy of the king and his efforts

similarity, however, is really remote; the story is a commonplace

We are left, therefore, to accept the view that the author who
wrote up the Cérudatta, and combined with it a new play,-
thought it well to conceal his identity and to pass off the work

5. Lhe Metres

The author of the Mycchakatikaé shows considerable skill in
metrical handling ; his favourite metre is naturally enough the
Cloka, which suits his rapid style and is adapted to further the
progress of the dialogue. It occurs 83 times, while the next
favourite, the pretty Vasantatilaka, appears 39 times, and the
Cardilavikridita 32 times. The only other important metres
are the Indravajra (26), with the Vancastha (9), and the Upajati
combination of both (5). But there occur also the Puspitagra,
Praharsini, Malini, Vidyunmala,? Vaigvadevi, Cikharini, Sragdhara,
and Harini, and one irregular stanza. Of the Arya there are 21
cases, including one Giti, with 30 morae in each half stanza, and
there are two instances of the Aupacchandasika, The Prakrit
metres show considerable variety ; of the Arya type theie are 5 3

1. The Date of Kilidisa

It is unfortunate, though as in the case of Shakespeare not
surprising, that we know practically nothing of the life and age
of Kalidasa save what we can infer from his works and from the
general history of Sanskrit literature. There are indeed stories?
of his ignorance in youth, until he was given poetic power by the

which is not one prema facze to be expected in the case of a poet

culture. But these tales are late and worthless, and equally
Without value is the fiction that he was a contemporary of King
Bhoja of Dhara in the first half of the eleventh century A.D.

ported by the earliest evidence, and totally without value.’
